articles.title_orig: EXPLAINER - Why is the world’s top chipmaker caught in a US-China spy row?
articles.title_zh: EXPLAINER - Why is the world’s top chipmaker caught in a US-China spy row?
articles.content_orig:
US tech giant Nvidia, the world's second-most valuable publicly traded company after Apple and a leading supplier of chips powering the global artificial intelligence boom, has found itself at the epicenter of a national security storm.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an extramarital relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence officials reportedly believe was recruited to gather information for Beijing.
The company announced an independent investigation Sunday, while US lawmakers have demanded answers about whether sensitive technology or information may have been exposed.
Beijing on Monday dismissed the allegations as “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears against China.”
“The so-called Chinese spy allegation is groundless. It is nothing but a smear against China,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
The controversy comes just days before US President Donald Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in China, where trade and technology remain major issues between the world's two largest economies.
Here is what is known so far.
The case centers on Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who worked as an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, a customer of Nvidia.
The story broke on Oct. 29. Citing people briefed on classified intelligence, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies had concluded Alice Huang was passing information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with Jensen Huang.
According to the report, US agencies had been monitoring her as part of a probe into whether Megaspeed was helping Chinese companies get around American export controls.
During that surveillance, they found she was in contact with an American citizen, later identified as the Nvidia chief.
The Times said Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago but took no action. It also said Jensen Huang never received a so-called defensive briefing, a warning sometimes given to people targeted by foreign spies.
Further US media reports said that US intelligence believed she had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to obtain information about advanced American chip technology and potentially influence US policy on chip exports to China.
On Sunday, Jensen Huang acknowledged the affair in a message to Nvidia employees, apologizing to his family and colleagues.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.
Huang also pledged to cooperate with Nvidia's investigation. “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security."
The board said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, would oversee the inquiry.
“While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” it said.
The board added that it still had confidence in Huang, who will keep leading the company during the probe.
In response to media reports, Beijing has denied any espionage.
Nvidia, based in Santa Clara, California, designs graphics processing units, or GPUs, the chips that have become the backbone of modern AI systems. Demand for them made Nvidia the first company to pass $5 trillion in market value, in October 2025.
Jensen Huang, 63, was born in Taiwan, moved to the US as a child and co-founded Nvidia in 1993. He has led the company ever since.
He has become one of the most influential business figures in Washington, building close ties with President Donald Trump and lobbying against strict limits on chip sales to China.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and is not related to Jensen Huang.
According to The New York Times, she spent much of her career in mainland China, including as a television reporter for Chinese state media and as a private banker.
She became a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips, builds data centers in Southeast Asia and rents out their computing power.
The Times reported that Megaspeed was formed in 2023 after splitting from a Chinese gaming company.
Citing trade data, the newspaper said a Malaysian affiliate of Megaspeed bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026.
The controversy comes at a delicate moment for the world’s two largest economies, which are competing for leadership in AI while trying to stabilize trade ties.
Huang has also been a fixture of US-China summitry. He joined Trump’s delegation to Beijing in May for talks with President Xi Jinping. He was also a guest at the White House state dinner Trump hosted for Xi in September.
The next meeting between the two leaders is expected at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18-19, where technology is likely to be on the agenda.
Speaking to reporters Sunday before leaving Florida, Trump was asked whether Huang would join him on the trip. “I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him,” he said.
US president also said he had not discussed the allegations with Huang but defended the Nvidia chief.
“I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump said, adding that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country.”
Huang faces a Nov. 11 deadline to tell House lawmakers whether he will attend the closed-door briefing.
The requested briefing falls on Nov. 18, the opening day of the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.
Huang, who heads a leading AI chipmaker and is an ally of President Donald Trump , apologized in a message to the company, saying, “I was unfaithful to my wife” and took "full responsibility" for his actions.
“My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Nvidia announced in a press release Sunday that its board was opening an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The company said that while its board had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information.
It said that the board has confidence in Huang and his ⁠leadership team, adding that the CEO fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.
Late last month, the New York Times reported that Huang had formed a close relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive at a Singapore-based data center.
Alice Huang is considered by U.S. officials to be a Chinese spy, feeding information to Beijing, according to the report, which cited sources briefed on the surveillance of Alice Huang and other officials and industry experts.
When asked about Alice Huang being suspected of spying for China, Liu Chang, the spokesman for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, told the Times the U.S. was pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against the Asian country.
Trump said on Sunday he had not spoken to Huang about ​the allegations, but ⁠called him a fine person.
"I hope everything's fine. He's done such an ‌incredible job," he added.
When asked if he believed he should have acted on intelligence when he was briefed about it, Trump said: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it."
Nvidia is one of the hottest companies in the stock market right now, given the popularity of its chips. It has a market capitalization of roughly 4.5 trillion and was trading at nearly $240 per share early last month.
However, the investigation adds to pressure on Nvidia at a time investors are already pulling back amid uncertainty over the sustainability of the booming AI market.
Nvidia shares fell in out-of-hours trading on Monday and extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference set to begin this week.
But Seoul expects contracted deliveries of Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) to proceed without disruption despite a controversy surrounding Huang. Vice Minister of Science and ICT Ryu Jemyung told a parliamentary budget committee that 10,000 GPUs funded under a 2025 supplementary budget had already arrived and were in use.
Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told the Times on Sunday that “today’s news will not slow Nvidia”. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.”
Huang, like other tech leaders, has flocked to Trump as the president embraces AI. The Nvidia leader and his wife, Lori Huang, attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September. His attendance wasn’t unusual, given that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg were also there.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to say whether Huang was excluded from U.S. briefings in light of the recent reporting. He told reporters Sunday before departing for France, “I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.”
Trump is a major backer of AI, trying to rebrand the technology as SI for “Super Intelligence” and loosen regulations.
While Huang may be an ally to the president, it will be hard to overlook a potential security breach from not only a U.S. adversary, but also its top competitor in the AI race.
“We’re leading China in AI,” the president said in September amid concerns that AI could pose an existential threat to humans . “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.”
Billionaire investor Bill Ackman said on X that the Nvidia CEO was an "incredible human," but if "indeed this is more ⁠than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem."
"I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security," he added.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk commented "I agree" on a post by Sequoia partner Shaun Maguire that said Huang "did something incredibly dumb" that was "bad for America" but that "Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership".
The Independent has reached out to the State Department and the White House for comment.

articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang's Reported Ties To A Suspected Chinese Spy Put Trump's Purchase Of Up To $5 Million In Nvidia Stock Back In The Spotlight - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares were down around 5% in premarket trading Monday after the tech giant launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
U.S. intelligence agencies said Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company Megaspeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and The Financial Times.
Nvidia said its board has launched an independent investigation following the reports that Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," the company said in a Sunday statement .
The co-founder and CEO told staff in an email that he had "fallen short" of his responsibility to serve his colleagues, the board, partners and shareholders around the world.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang said in the email.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" was unsubstantiated, Reuters reported.
Nvidia was last trading down 5.2% in premarket trading.
The key question for investors will be whether Huang will remain as CEO, according to Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons," Ives said in a Sunday note.
"There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the Board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally. This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China which remains a key battleground issue in DC," Ives added.
Tech stocks took a hammering last week as investors reassessed the data center build-out after Democrats won control of Congress.
Asian tech stocks rose across the region on Monday, rebounding from Friday's losses. Shares of U.S. chipmakers were slightly lower in premarket trading, with Intel , Marvell , Qualcomm and Arm all down over 1%.
Joachim Klement, investment strategist at Panmure Liberum, said the impact is currently contained to Nvidia.
But if Huang's position is "endangered," then "Nvidia might cut back on supporting other companies, whether it's in Asia or in the U.S., that might then spread a little bit more into the other semiconductor names," he said.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday praised Huang's leadership but said he hadn't spoken to the CEO about the investigation.
"I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it," the president told reporters.
"He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump added.
Shaun Maguire, partner at Sequoia, also defended the tech giant CEO, saying in a post on X that Huang is "one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation."
He added: "two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership."
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk reshared Maguire's post, adding that he agrees with the venture capitalist's statements.
Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month.
— CNBC's Kif Leswing and Kamaron McNair helped contribute to this report.

Edited by Caitlin Doherty and Owen Amos with reporting from Tessa Wong and Laura Bicker
US tech giant Nvidia is one of the world's mot valuable companies.
As CEO Jensen Huang is now facing an investigation amid claims he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, here are some key things to know about the firm:
What does Nvidia do? It's a leading provider of advanced computer chips and provides this technology to major firms such as OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, and Meta.
Why is it so important? Essentially every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, Microsoft, use Nvidia chips.
Its chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, who are locked in an AI race - with America having long been concerned about Beijing's access to advanced computing technology.
The CEO of technology manufacturer Logitech has reacted to claims that Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Asked how big a concern allegations of spying by China are within the tech industry, Hanneke Faber tells  the BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think every country, every company is always trying to gain an edge."
She adds Logitech is "super focused" on privacy, security and making sure data in its products and development plans "are safe from the world".
She says that "in the world of AI - privacy security, cyber security are definitely more important than ever. And we are dedicating mores resources to that than ever".
The Chinese Foreign Ministry would not comment further on claims that the CEO of the tech giant Nvidia had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun tells reporters at the regular daily press briefing that he had already responded to the allegations.
He says: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he couldn't comment on Jensen Huang, as he spoke to press on the tarmac in Homestead, Florida before flying to Paris for the G7 meeting.
One journalist asked Rubio during the gaggle on Sunday about whether Huang was cut out of any US government meetings.
Rubio replied: "I can't comment on any of that. I just can't comment because of the nature of it. And I also can't comment on an internal corporate matter that's going on with Nvidia, as you highlight, I don't know anything about that part of it so."
The secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo warning the Trump administration about the relationship between the Nvidia chief and Chinese businesswoman, last spring.
Jensen Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners.
They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.
In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation.
The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.
Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.
Lily Jamali North America Technology Correspondent
Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race.
Which is why Jensen Huang's affair - with someone US officials had reportedly concluded was a Chinese spy - has prompted national security concerns among American lawmakers .
The US's advantage in the AI race lies in companies like Nvidia, which designs some of the most sophisticated AI chips on the planet.
Since 2022 the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.
But this means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the lucrative Chinese market.
Despite his ostensible closeness to Trump, Huang has also not been able to get the administration's blessings to sell chips to China.
Huang has been a vocal advocate for US-China dialogue on AI development. But his words have cut no ice with the Trump administration, which has consistently framed the AI race as a matter of national security.
Nvidia's board of directors said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised" .
As for Huang, he has said that he's committed to "supporting America's national security" .
Peter Hoskins Business reporter, Singapore
Jensen Huang and his wife Lori at an awards ceremony in California in April
A short while ago, I spoke with Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine - a biography on Jensen Huang - about the impact of this revelation on Huang's carefully crafted public persona.
"Jensen in my conversations with him and in other conversations has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man. That's very important to him," Witt told me.
"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways. Both of his children work for Nvidia - Spencer and Maddison."
Witt adds that "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
Shares in Nvidia  are expected to fall when trading starts in New York later.
Overnight trading indicates that the AI chip giant will open about 4% lower.
With a stock market valuation of around $4.5tn, Nvidia is one of the the world's most valuable companies.

But in the past, Megaspeed had been suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in an evasion of export controls.
After reports recently surfaced in the New York Times about a relationship between its boss Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, Nvidia said it was aware that Megaspeed had been probed for helping divert Nvidia chips to China, in an evasion of US export controls, but maintains those allegations were probed and debunked.

articles.title_orig: Tens of thousands march in Amsterdam, pressing the Dutch government on Gaza and Israel
articles.title_zh: Tens of thousands march in Amsterdam, pressing the Dutch government on Gaza and Israel
articles.content_orig:
More than 200,000 people have taken to the streets of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, demanding government action against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the Dutch branch of Amnesty International, one of the organisers.
Sunday’s ‘Red Line’ protesters, many wearing red items of clothing, called for tighter trade restrictions on Israel and a halt to all arms sales.
“What is happening there is inhumane,” Mike van Dongen said as he walked in the huge throng of people.
“As far as I’m concerned, [the Dutch authorities] are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”
As the protesters marched along a normally busy Amsterdam street that was closed to traffic on Sunday, a man stood at a bus stop with a loudspeaker shouting, “Free, free Palestine!” Many of the marchers echoed his cry as they passed.
Israel’s genocidal war has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, since October 2023.
Sunday’s protest was similar to one in early October last year. That followed ‘Red Line’ demonstrations last June when protesters marched through the streets of The Hague.
A “ ceasefire ” took effect in Gaza on October 10 last year, but Israeli attacks and killings have continued on an almost-daily basis since.
The war in Gaza has strained relations between the Netherlands and Israel. The Dutch foreign minister resigned last year after failing to secure new sanctions against Israel.
Since then, a new minority coalition government took power in February and introduced an import ban on products from Israeli settlements, which the Dutch government and most of the international community consider illegal – the ban provoked a diplomatic spat with Israel.
Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who took part in a march last year but was not present on Sunday, defended his government’s actions at his weekly news conference on Friday.
“Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there,” he said.
He added that his administration is “exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure” on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza.

articles.title_orig: Air France A350 Nearly Collides Midair With American A321 After Wrong Turn At LAX
articles.title_zh: Air France A350 Nearly Collides Midair With American A321 After Wrong Turn At LAX
articles.content_orig:
Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.
This article was updated on Monday, November 9, 2026, to include new details on the unauthorized turn and a similar 2025 incident. It was originally published on Sunday, November 8, 2026.
Two aircraft belonging to American Airlines and Air France came within 400 feet (121 meters) of vertical separation as both jets departed from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). Quick actions by air traffic control and the pilots onboard averted a close call that could have had catastrophic consequences .
The two planes were departing from California's busiest airport in the early hours of Saturday morning. Air France Flight 28 was heading for Papeete (PPT), while American Flight 1660 was flying to Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW). The two jets — which collectively could have been carrying more than 500 passengers — came dangerously close to each other shortly after takeoff, before controllers intervened to prevent a potential collision.
The Air France Airbus A350-900 , operating as AF28 , had been cleared to take off from Los Angeles via the SUMMR2 procedure. SUMMR2, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), is a set route that tells departing aircraft which direction to fly after takeoff. In this case, planes taking off from Runways 24L/R and 25L/R must initially climb straight ahead before following their assigned route.
At the same time, the American jet, destined for Texas , was told by air traffic control to stay at 2,000 feet, to allow the Air France widebody to turn and then head to FL270. However, an unauthorized turn by the Air France aircraft brought the two jets onto conflicting flight paths.
Simple Flying reached out to Air France for comment on the incident; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.
According to TurbineTraveler on X , the Air France plane made an unauthorized turn left shortly after takeoff, rather than continuing straight as instructed. This placed the A350 directly in the trajectory of the departing American jet. This led the two planes to come within dangerous proximity of each other, known as a loss of separation event.
The controller quickly spotted the developing conflict and instructed both aircraft to turn away from each other. The controller then questioned the Air France crew about the deviation from its departure route. Both aircraft involved are detailed in the table below, with flight data captured from the Simple Flying Flight Tracker :
Both the American and Air France flights were then able to continue safely to their intended destinations with no reported injuries or harm to anyone on board. A similar incident occurred in Los Angeles in 2025, when an American and ITA Airways jet almost collided midair after a pilot deviation from the busy airport.
So far, reports indicate that neither crew received a Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) resolution advisory, an automated cockpit warning that instructs pilots to climb or descend to avoid another aircraft. These alerts can prevent midair collisions when aircraft get too close, giving pilots immediate instructions to increase their separation.
Since the incident was first reported, outlets have published different figures for how close AF28 and AA1660 came to each other. According to The Aviation Herald , the A350 began turning left while climbing through 1,800 feet, despite its departure procedure calling for a straight climb to 5,000 feet.
The incident also bears striking similarities to an event involving ITA Airways in October 2025, when a Rome-bound Airbus A330-900 departing Runway 24L turned left toward an American A321 that had taken off from Runway 25R.
As one of the busiest airports in the US and the world, Los Angeles International Airport has carefully controlled departure routes to keep aircraft safely separated. The SUMMR2 procedure directs westbound departures out over the Pacific Ocean, helping keep them clear of other departing and arriving traffic.
Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.
SUMMR flights often transition to long-haul or coastal routes, including to destinations in Hawaii , Asia, and the north, like San Francisco . Instead of following this procedure, the Air France pilot made a sharp left turn shortly after departure, which intersected the path of the American jet that had departed from Runway 25R . Fortunately, the departure controller identified the conflict, and their swift actions resulted in the two planes being able to quickly change course and avoid a midair collision.

articles.title_zh: Passenger trains crash in Egypt, killing 7 and injuring 125, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.
The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.
The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.
Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.
Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.
Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.

Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
Russian forces conducted a second consecutive day of missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s critical and energy infrastructure overnight on November 7 to 8, causing widespread power outages. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces launched 164 strike drones, including 112 jet-powered drones, and three Kh-59/69 cruise missiles overnight, and that Ukrainian forces intercepted 137 drones.[1] The Ukrainian Energy Ministry and Ukrainian officials reported on November 8 that Russian forces struck several energy facilities, resulting in power outages in Dnipropetrovsk, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv, Odesa and Chernihiv oblasts, and prompting rolling blackouts throughout northern and central Ukraine.[2] The Ukrainian Energy Ministry added that Dnipropetrovsk Oblast faced the most severe power outages due to damage to energy infrastructure and that power restrictions remained in place in Kyiv City following the November 6 to 7 drone and missile strike series. Ukrainian officials stated on November 8 that Russian strikes against energy infrastructure left 600,000 people without power in Dnipro City and Dnipropetrovsk Oblast; and 140 high-rise buildings in Zhytomyr Oblast without heat.[3] The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed on November 8 that Russian forces struck a substation near Biloshytsi, Zhytomyr Oblast overnight on November 7 to 8, and the Kamyanske substation in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on the afternoon of November 8.[4]
Russia continues to leverage its Winter 2026-2027 strike campaign to degrade Ukrainian energy security and disrupt civilian life, highlighting Ukraine’s urgent need for capabilities to defend against and degrade Russia’s ability to launch large strike packages.[5] German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius stated on November 7 that Germany has exhausted available Patriot interceptor stockpiles for transfer to Ukraine, highlighting the global interceptor shortage that is impeding Ukraine’s ability to secure interceptors necessary to defend against Russian ballistic missiles.[6] Ukrainian forces are now increasingly targeting missile launch sites and ballistic missile production sites in Russia to reduce Russia’s ability to launch such devastating strikes as Ukraine’s air defense stockpiles continue to dwindle, underscoring the importance of ensuring Ukraine has sufficient long-range strike capabilities to prevent Russia from launching combined strike packages.
Russian forces reportedly suffered a nearly 450,000 death toll in Ukraine since February 2022, which does not include wounded, missing, or foreign personnel. Belarusian pro-opposition and pro-Ukrainian hacker groups claimed on November 7 that they hacked into the Russian Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) and found that Russian authorities registered at least 440,982 deceased Russian servicemembers from February 2022 through the end of August 2026.[7] The hacker groups specified that Rosstat attributed about 356,000 deaths to “war operations” and the remaining deaths to other war-related causes including “military operations” and “terrorist acts;” causes vaguely related to or not specified directly as combat. Rosstat reportedly also registered some deaths in occupied Ukraine that did not have a specified cause, and non-combat deaths of servicemembers including suicides, road accidents, and illness. The hackers noted that this figure does not include wounded, missing, or casualties among foreign mercenaries. The hackers assessed that the total Russian death toll is over 450,100 deaths, including 9,118 personnel who died for unspecified reasons outside of occupied Ukraine. ISW is unable to verify the groups’ findings, but the reporting is relatively consistent with Russian opposition sources Mediazona and Meduza’s joint investigation, which independently confirmed over 285,000 Russian deaths and estimated over 350,000 registered deaths as of November 2026.[8] The actual number of Russian servicemembers killed in action (KIA) is likely much higher, as both the hacker groups’ and Meduza and Mediazona’s figures are very likely a conservative estimate due to reporting limitations. Russian officials have also tried to misrepresent the total number of deceased servicemembers by registering them as missing in action (MIA).[9] Total Russian casualties (killed or seriously wounded) are reportedly nearly 1.6 million as of November 2026, and Russian forces experienced their highest monthly casualties throughout the war in October 2026.[10] Russia’s increasing casualties come as Russian forces have suffered more casualties than they have been able to recruit as of July 2026.
The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) signaled that logistics remain a significant challenge for Russian forces, but it remains unclear whether the MoD can meaningfully resolve it. Russian Deputy Defense Minister Colonel General Valery Solodchuk, who officially took his post as deputy defense minister for rear-area logistics on November 6, outlined the Russian MoD’s two main priorities for logistics in a speech on November 8.[11] Solodchuk stated that the Russian MoD’s primary focus is on using unmanned systems to conduct logistics in the “kill zone” — the roughly 30-kilometer zone behind the frontline wherein Ukrainian drones can strike Russian troops, vehicles, and logistics, impeding movement.[12] Solodchuk also identified rear-area logistics as the Russian MoD’s other priority and stated that the Russian MoD is creating a unified system intended to allow Russian commanders real-time visibility into rear-area logistics services.[13] Solodchuk also postured the Russian MoD as already effectively solving some logistics issues from Ukraine’s strike campaigns, claiming that the MoD has “resolved” the objective of defending rear-area facilities, warehouses, and arsenals by strengthening different aspects of Russia’s air defense umbrella.[14]
Ukrainian forces have been intensifying their intermediate- and long-range strike campaigns for much of 2026, particularly against Russian logistics arteries and defense production facilities. It remains unclear if the Russian MoD could adequately counteract Ukrainian strikes, however, and Russian milbloggers continue to identify shortfalls in these Russian efforts. A Russian milblogger responded to Ukrainian strikes against a bridge along the M-14 Rostov-Crimea highway in Rostov Oblast on November 8, noting that Ukrainian forces continue expanding the geography of their interdiction campaign and that strikes against roadway bridges complicate Russian logistics.[15] Another milblogger complained that Russian authorities have not been transparent about Ukrainian rear-area strikes and that the lack of transparency degrades public trust in Russian authorities.[16]
We do not report in detail on Russian war crimes because these activities are well-covered in Western media and do not directly affect the military operations we are assessing and forecasting. We will continue to evaluate and report on the effects of these criminal activities on the Ukrainian military and the Ukrainian population and specifically on combat in Ukrainian urban areas. We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.
Ukrainian forces likely struck Russian logistics infrastructure in Rostov Oblast overnight on November 7 to 8. articles.title_orig: Saudi Aramco Tower Targeted in Rare Strike on Riyadh Finance Hub
articles.title_zh: Saudi Aramco Tower Targeted in Rare Strike on Riyadh Finance Hub
articles.content_orig:
The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in the Saudi Arabian capital's central financial district, had been hit by an air attack.
A statement issued via the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh's business zone on Saturday, without mentioning the Aramco Tower by name.
The Saudi energy ministry said the tower had suffered only "minor damage" and no one had been killed or injured.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows more extensive damage to the building, with at least one floor appearing to have been badly hit by a missile or drone strike.
Windows on more than one level appear to have been shattered by the strike.
The Houthis also said Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities were targeted in separate strikes. Saudi Arabia said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several missiles.
The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based armed group against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia, which the Gulf power has struggled to contain in recent months.
It came a day after the Houthis accused a Saudi-led coalition of killing at least 33 people , including women and children, in an air strike on Yemen.
Footage broadcast by Houthi-run television channel Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
Saba said 39 people had been injured in the strike. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.
Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting has intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.
An informal ceasefire unravelled in July after the Tehran-backed Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport Saudi Arabia said had been to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing there.
Major fighting has since resumed between Houthi forces and troops aligned with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

articles.title_orig: Democrat triumph offers China ‘window to catch up’ on AI
articles.title_zh: Democrat triumph offers China ‘window to catch up’ on AI
articles.content_orig:
Council on Foreign Relations
Joshua Kurlantzick is an expert on U.S.-China relations, South and Southeast Asian politics and economics, and is the author of ‘ Beijing’s Global Media Offensive: China’s Uneven Campaign To Influence Asia and the World .’
Following the Democratic Party’s dramatic and massive sweep of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate on Tuesday, Asian leaders, as is their custom, have said little publicly. They stayed mum even though the Democrats won the overall House popular vote by the biggest margin in more than fifty years. China just called for cooperation with the United States, and no Southeast Asian leader has commented at all publicly on the results. But in private, many leaders are relieved.
The Iran war has been particularly challenging for the United States’ Asian partners and allies, and they hope that after the midterm results U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision-making on the issue will become more predictable. Some think he could even move more quickly toward winding down the war, which has roiled Asian energy markets—Asia relies more on oil and liquefied natural gas from the Persian Gulf than any other part of the world.
Several reasons support this hope, including the renewed pressure on U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, the Trump advisor who is believed to be most in favor of the war and who is unloved in Asia . Already, some lame-duck Republican senators and representatives want Hegseth gone: retiring Senator Thom Tillis (R-NC) said Tuesday night that Hegseth, who has faced criticism from members of both parties, would soon face “a reckoning,” while outgoing Representative Thomas Massie (R-KY) had filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. Democratic leaders, too, have their eyes on getting rid of the secretary of defense, who has overseen a tumultuous period at the Pentagon marked by the firings of senior military officials .
Ahead of the midterms, Trump had urged voters to pretend he was on the ballot and to treat the vote as a referendum on him and his policies. Apparently they did , and the Republican Party is now in disarray. Amid the upheaval after the election, many who have stayed quiet are going to speak up under a lame-duck president. One of them, Vice President JD Vance, who had long been a skeptic of the war against Iran , has already posted a long statement on X that bluntly said: “The reason we lost is the war.”
The relief for Asian allies could extend beyond any rethinking of the Iran war. Congress has historically been a strong supporter of issues critical to Asian partners and allies, including a tougher approach toward China and arms sales to Taiwan; relieved Taiwanese officials quickly noted after the elections that the U.S.-Taiwan relationship has strong bipartisan support in Congress. (Even before the midterms, in September, the bipartisan Senate Taiwan Caucus had urged Trump to move forward with $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan, which the island would pay for itself.) The White House had recently taken a soft approach toward China, a position that was unpopular with some Republicans and many Democrats. The new Congress will likely put more pressure on the Trump administration to take a clearer and tougher approach on a range of issues, including Chinese artificial intelligence and export restrictions.
The new Congress will likely put more pressure on the Trump administration to take a clearer and tougher approach on a range of issues.
Japanese and Philippine officials I have spoken with, meanwhile, believed that with much more pushback from Congress, Trump will be forced to stop slamming Asian partners and allies with tariffs. Indeed, most Asian policymakers I have interviewed since the election believed that, with polls showing so many Americans recognizing the links between tariff policy and higher prices, and voicing their strong dislike of tariffs , the White House will change course. Even if Trump does want to continue applying tariffs, the jockeying for the Republican nomination in 2028 has essentially already begun, and ending the unpopular fixation on tariffs is in the interests of those wanting to succeed Trump.
But the forty-seventh president is nothing if not unpredictable. A lame-duck Trump could be dangerous . Already isolated from external voices—Trump reportedly relies heavily on close aides who cherry-pick and print out favorable news and social media posts for his review—he could become even more alienated from advisors such as Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump has always said that his “gut” is smarter than anyone else’s brain.
Asian leaders will find out fairly quickly—on many levels—whether their hopes for improved relations with the United States are reality or fantasy. Trump is scheduled to arrive in Manila on November 16 for the summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and related meetings. By then, he could well have ignored Vance and others and renewed attacks on Iran. After all, even following the election, he said he did not regret launching the conflict and that he would have “done it again.” Such a move would be profoundly dangerous militarily for the United States, which is already low on many munitions . But diplomatically, it would also all but seal the United States’ long-term unpopularity in Asia.

articles.title_orig: China Producer Inflation Accelerates as Consumer Prices Cool
articles.title_zh: China Producer Inflation Accelerates as Consumer Prices Cool
articles.content_orig:
Producer prices in China grew at the fastest rate since June 2022, accelerating for the third month in a row.
The PPI for October came in at 5.7%, compared to the 5.3% expected by economists polled by Reuters. The increase was driven by a sharp rise in prices in the mining and raw materials industries.
The increase was driven by very strong external demand, Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ."
Consumer inflation in China slowed to 0.7% in October, its first deceleration after two straight months of increases.
The figure missed expectations of a 0.8% rise from economists polled by Reuters, and was lower than the 0.9% seen in September.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, came in at 0.8%, down from the 1% seen in the month before.
The rise in consumer prices were still held up by prices of gasoline, which was the largest contributor to the increase in prices, but this was offset by a sharper than expected fall in food prices, according to Dong Lijuan, chief statistician of the urban division at China's National Bureau of Statistics.
The Chinese economy has shown some signs of expansion recently. It grew faster than expected in the third quarter, and September saw a sharp beat in retail sales.
The mainland Chinese CSI 300 index gained 0.56% after the data release.
Pinpoint's Zhang said that domestic demand has been rather weak due to the property market, and this is a key reason why inflation is not picking up in China "There's no clear sign of stabilization [in that sector] yet," he said, adding this was weighing on the household consumer confidence and local government revenue.
"So the the overall economic momentum has been weak and hasn't really seen [a] clear sign of recovery," Zhang explained.

Democrats won several key races in the high-stakes midterm elections -- with ABC News projecting that Democrats will take control of the Senate and the House.
Attorney General Todd Blanche suggested in an interview Sunday that there could be investigations of Democrats pushing oversight probes into President Donald Trump's administration, despite no evidence that such calls could amount to criminal threats.
"It depends on what's said. So, yes, there could be," Blanche said in an interview on CNN's "State of the Union" program, when asked if there could be such investigations.
"You have free speech in this country. You are allowed to be critical of President Trump, of me, of this administration. But when the threats become so vile and so dangerous that you are telling people in college that they better be careful if they want to work in the Trump administration because somebody will come after them, at some point, you have to draw the line," Blanche said.
Blanche's comments follow Trump's social media post on Saturday directing the Justice Department to investigate Democrats who have previewed plans for aggressive oversight probes into administration officials following Tuesday's midterms.
-ABC News' Alexander Mallin

articles.title_zh: Trump to meet Qatari prime minister about mediation efforts with Iran
articles.content_orig:
Qatar, which has been mediating between the United States and Iran, says the two countries remain engaged in talks aimed at ending their conflict. US President Donald Trump indicated on Thursday that he would soon decide whether to launch additional attacks against Iran.
In a statement issued on Saturday, Qatar said its mediators remain in close coordination with both sides to support negotiations toward an agreement.
US news site Axios reported that mediators are continuing discussions with Tehran and Washington to take a series of steps over two days in an effort to build mutual confidence. According to the report, proposed measures include the United States lifting its naval blockade and unfreezing some Iranian funds in exchange for Iran allowing inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency to enter the country.
Qatar's Amir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, reportedly spoke by phone with Trump about ways to de-escalate tensions in the region.
Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that he had spoken with counterparts from 12 countries over the previous 48 hours, including officials from Qatar and fellow mediator Pakistan. He said he used the conversations to explain Iran's position on the military operations carried out by the United States and Israel.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Trump asked Netanyahu to move on Gaza peace plan in post-election call
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Trump asked Netanyahu to move on Gaza peace plan in post-election call
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON / RIYADH/TEHRAN: President Donald Trump told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call Thursday that he wants him to take steps to implement his Gaza peace plan, Axios reported citing two sources with knowledge of the matter.
The roadmap calls for disarming Hamas and demilitarising Gaza, as well as transferring responsibility for governing the enclave to a new Palestinian technocratic government. But it has been on hold for months because of the Israeli elections held on Oct 27.
The Trump administration did not want implementation of the plan to become a politically explosive issue during the Israeli election campaign. Trump endorsed Netanyahu shortly before the election. Now that it’s over, the president wants to forge ahead with his Gaza plan, regardless of whether Netanyahu or his opposition forms a new government.
A year ago, Israel and Hamas agreed to the first phase of Trump’s 20-point plan, which led to a ceasefire in the Gaza war and the release of the last 20 living hostages taken during the Oct 7, 2023 attacks.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio as well as Kushner and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff also participated in the call between the president and Netanyahu.
A source with knowledge of the details described the call, which Netanyahu initiated, as constructive. It also addressed the war in Iran. The White House and the Israeli prime minister’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A day after the call, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who is a member of the Board of Peace, visited Israel. He met with Netanyahu and his opponent Gadi Eisenkot, who’s been tasked with trying to form a new government to replace Netanyahu’s.  A source with knowledge of the visit said Blair urged Netanyahu and other Israeli political leaders to give the plan a chance.
“The implementation will be difficult but we believe it is a good plan for Israel. Nevertheless we can’t do it with one hand tied behind our back,” the U.S. official said. “We want to move forward collaboratively and we need full cooperation and partnership from the Israeli government,” the person added.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump on Sunday said he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progress, CNN reported.
“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” CNN cited Trump as saying in a phone interview. “The answer is, highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary.” CNN did not specify exactly what it had asked Trump, who also said the US had identified potential infrastructure targets. These included 38 bridges “that we can knock down in literally one hour,” he said.
While Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that mediators striving for a peace deal between the US and Iran had not travelled at all since the “shock” of the US midterm elections.
“We now have to see how long it will take for them to digest these results, in order to determine how we are going to move forward,” the top Iranian diplomat told state TV following the elections in which the Republican Party of US President Donald Trump suffered heavy losses.
He said it would “take some time before the atmosphere is favourable for the resumption of mediator travel” and called for patience.
Earlier, Aragchi posted on X: “American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own.”
He called on Washington to accept previously articulated Iranian demands or “choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened warriors rain down hell”.
In September, Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen the strait, with demands including ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending its counter-blockade of Iranian ports. It later proposed doing so in just two days, an offer Araghchi repeated in his X post on Sunday.
Iranian media suggested explosions in southern Iran on Saturday evening were related to Iranian military activities rather than US strikes while both sides reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz.
Three oil tankers caught fire on Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran regularly targets ships that transit without its authorisation, the Revolutionary Guards said in a statement.
Emirati state media said on Sunday that 22 people had been rescued from a burning vessel in the Gulf of Oman and were in stable condition.
AFP was unable to confirm if the various reports referenced the same incidents. Iranian authorities executed three men on Sunday on charges linked to January 2026 protests, the judiciary said, after what rights groups described as an unfair trial.
Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHR) said the hangings at dawn of Hassan Divband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh in the city of Karaj outside Tehran brought the number of men hanged over the January protests to at least 39 and warned many more were at risk.
Israel is not finished with Iran, its defence minister said Sunday, as he also warned Tehran’s Lebanese ally Hezbollah to hold fire in any resumption of war.
Defence Minister Israel Katz renewed charges that Iran—attacked twice since last year in major Israeli-US bombing campaigns—is pursuing nuclear weapons, a claim that Tehran denies.
The US military has announced it will create a 20-member task force to find ways to disrupt land routes into Iran that it says are used for shipments of weapons and illicit materials.
The task force’s work “will further constrain Iran’s ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military,” US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said in a statement posted on X on Saturday.
Houthi authorities said on Sunday that Saudi strikes killed 33 people, many of them women and children, in Yemen’s Sanaa province, as deaths mount in the country’s revived civil war.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthis on Sunday claimed an attack on the financial district of the Saudi capital Riyadh, with eyewitnesses saying they saw damage to a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Aramco. “Aramco tower in KAFD has been targeted, that’s the sure thing,” an eyewitness told AFP, referring to the King Abdullah Financial District. Two other witnesses confirmed seeing damage to the building.
Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said an administrative building belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco in Riyadh had been damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries or fatalities reported.
The KAFD is one of the most visible manifestations of the kingdom’s ongoing economic and social reforms drive, with towering glass skyscrapers, high-end retail outlets and green spaces dotting the area.
Targeting the area, which is also home to residential buildings and a large metro station with heavy commuter traffic during the morning rush hour, would mark a major escalation by the Houthis.
The attack came hours after the kingdom’s education ministry announced the return of in-person schooling after weeks of remote learning in Riyadh.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said forces had “destroyed two ballistic missile launchers” in northern Yemen’s Saada that he said were used by the Houthis in Sunday’s “attempted attack” on Riyadh.
Earlier, Malki said air defences had destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh, as loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital.
Iran on Sunday condemned recent Saudi strikes in Yemen, including attacks on a market in Taiz province and the village of Al-Shariyah that reportedly killed dozens of civilians.

articles.title_orig: The Kremlin call: How talking to Putin exposed Europe’s deepest rift over Ukraine
articles.title_zh: The Kremlin call: How talking to Putin exposed Europe’s deepest rift over Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Beneath the chandeliers and oil paintings of his Presidential Palace, Finland’s president Alexander Stubb sat down next to his old friend Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian prime minister, to call Vladimir Putin.
They hoped such a dramatic and direct intervention with Russia’s leader would demonstrate European resolve.
Instead, the conversation on a damp autumn morning in Helsinki triggered the biggest rift among Nordic allies since Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine — and exposed Europe’s wider divisions over how to deal with Moscow at a pivotal moment in the push for peace.
As Russian and Ukrainian negotiators prepare for talks with Donald Trump’s envoys in Abu Dhabi this week, the fallout from the call is still reverberating across Europe. Governments are arguing over who should represent Europe in future negotiations and remain divided over a question at the heart of the debate: Does engaging Putin help deliver peace, or simply reward aggression?
Underlying European anxiety is another dilemma: Can America be trusted to broker a fair deal for them and most of all for Ukraine?
EU leaders will grapple with these questions at an informal summit in Dublin this week. Few involved expect them to agree.
In an interview with POLITICO in Oslo, Støre explained why he and Stubb decided to call a leader waging hybrid warfare on Europe and killing Ukrainian civilians with daily drone and missile strikes.
“We work closely with our European partners in supporting Ukraine, but the only voice reaching Moscow comes from Washington,” Støre said. “And you know, we have good and open relations with the American negotiators, with the American administration, but this [war] happens in Europe. And living month by month, thinking that this war will end by Europe not talking to Moscow, I think, is an illusion.”
Other countries sharing a border — and a history —  with Putin’s Russia profoundly disagree.
“Europe should not be in a mediator’s position,” Estonia’s Prime Minister Kristen Michal told POLITICO in another interview . “You should not take the role of trying to please the dictator.”
Based on interviews with politicians, diplomats and officials, many granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, this is the inside story of a phone call that shook Europe.
Europe has struggled for influence over the stop-start Ukraine peace process ever since Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, promptly picked up the phone to Putin and ended U.S. financial assistance to Kyiv.
Trump’s interventions shattered the transatlantic consensus built under his predecessor Joe Biden, offering Putin the prospect of an advantageous ceasefire and a return to the international fold.
The U.S.-Iran war this year interrupted momentum but Trump returned to the topic of Ukraine again in October, criticizing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for continuing to attack Russian energy infrastructure, while declaring that Putin’s side had been “fine”.
Fearing the negotiations were drifting toward collapse, Stubb and Støre intervened. Støre hosted Zelenskyy and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo in an attempt to repair relations. Stubb, who also attended, declared the meeting on Oct. 20 had put the peace process “back on track.”
But 24 hours later, Witkoff again stunned European leaders by meeting Putin in St. Petersburg and praising him as a “humanitarian.”
After consulting Zelenskyy, the two Nordic leaders concluded they could not leave Trump, Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner as the only Western figures speaking directly to Putin.
Stubb and Støre have known each other for years and worked closely on Russian affairs when they both served as foreign ministers. They talk and text frequently — and like to pair up on key files despite coming from different political backgrounds.
They had quietly explored the idea of a joint call to the Kremlin for months and concluded that reviving momentum would be critical ahead of renewed negotiations in Abu Dhabi.
Europeans, many officials privately acknowledge, no longer trusted Washington to defend either Europe’s interests or Ukraine’s.
“We have to ask the question in Europe if we feel that someone else should have the contact and the discussion on our behalf,” one EU government official said. “Is the feeling that the U.S. should own our objectives?”
“It’s important that Donald Trump is not the only leader from the West who talks to Putin,” another senior European official said. “We need pro-Ukraine leaders putting their messages to Putin too.”
So, almost five years after Russia’s diplomatic isolation began, Stubb and Støre decided to call the Kremlin. The Nordic team reached out to Putin’s officials and agreed parameters for the conversation. Each side would take turns to deliver their prepared messages, without interruption from the other.
Some of the omens were inauspicious from the start.
As the leaders sat next to each other at the long cabinet table in Stubb’s plush presidential salon on Oct. 27, two large, gilt-framed oil paintings loomed over them, depicting battle scenes from the Crimean War. One canvas shows an Anglo-French naval force retreating under fire on Finnish territory, a reminder of an era two centuries ago when Finland itself was part of the Russian Empire.
According to some accounts, Putin shared his own keen interest in Russia’s past with the two Nordic leaders — delivering a lengthy lesson on Slavic history and the origins of the war in Ukraine.
One senior official familiar with the matter said Stubb and Støre listened patiently during the 90-minute conversation. Other European officials briefed on the call denied that Putin had given the two leaders a history lecture at all, and suggested this claim was Russian spin aimed at humiliating the Europeans.
Støre himself said: “I was present. He didn’t.” Putin has well-worn arguments about the origins of the war, he added. “But in all fairness, he can give his explanation, and we respond to that.”
For their part, the Nordic pair first gave Putin Zelenskyy’s messages — that territorial boundaries can only be discussed at leader level, face to face, and first there must be de-escalation measures. Stubb and his friend then turned to the matter of Baltic Sea security and the need to keep the waterway open for trade.
One reason for holding the call was to try to judge Putin’s state of mind, according to officials. The Norwegian leader said Putin was “rational” and “professional” on the phone. “His arguments were perfectly clearly transmitted.”
Putin took the idea of talks in Abu Dhabi seriously and told the Nordic pair he would instruct his negotiators to prepare for the meeting to explore if progress is possible. “The fact that he picks up that phone, that we have, you know, other ways of reaching, I think that signals, at least that there’s a readiness to sit down.”
But afterwards, Støre was still not convinced that Putin was genuinely open to a deal. Despite their efforts, the Norwegian and Finnish team do not expect a major breakthrough in Abu Dhabi.
When Stubb’s office announced the surprise call had happened, the diplomatic blowback played out live in public.
By coincidence, the leaders of Denmark and Sweden, among others, were already gathered in Helsinki for a Nordic Council meeting. Confronted by TV crews, they made little effort to hide their irritation.
“I’m very skeptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative,” Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told broadcasters. “I think we should keep Europe united rather than going it alone.”
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said peace must come through “strength” rather than “appeasement”. Lithuania also criticized the move.
In private, some diplomats were even harsher. “There are too many middle-aged men who want to end up in the history books having solved this war,” one EU diplomat said. “Putin is just gaining from opening up a more normalized dialogue with the rest of the world — and continuing to bomb and kill i

articles.title_orig: Cruise ship pianist rescued from sea after nine hours in Pacific Ocean
articles.title_zh: Cruise ship pianist rescued from sea after nine hours in Pacific Ocean
articles.content_orig:
A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports.
Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in," Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him.
The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident.
The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas.
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from "a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water".
The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said.
Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered.
"It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean," Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS.
Norton credited the man's survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures.
"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water's 76 degrees," Norton said, which equates to about 24C.
"A different year, no way he makes it," Norton said.
The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average.
In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time.
"To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."

articles.title_orig: Iran acquires oil facilities in China to bypass US sanctions, leaked document shows
articles.title_zh: Iran acquires oil facilities in China to bypass US sanctions, leaked document shows
articles.content_orig:
Iran is using oil terminals and storage facilities in China to keep sanctioned tankers operating despite US restrictions, according to a confidential document obtained by Iran International and information from Oil Ministry sources.
The document is a confidential letter from Hamid Bovard, the former head of the National Iranian Oil Company and current acting oil minister, responding to a highly confidential letter Ali Shamkhani, a former secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, sent to then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei.
Shamkhani, who served as Khamenei's political adviser, had described oil sales under President Masoud Pezeshkian as disastrous. Both Shamkhani and Khamenei were killed in US-Israeli strikes on February 28, 2026.
In his letter, Bovard criticized the administration of former President Ebrahim Raisi for its policy of using newer vessels and described an arrangement developed under Pezeshkian with what he characterized as covert cooperation from China.
According to Bovard, Iranian authorities instructed trusted oil intermediaries to continue using sanctioned vessels capable of docking at designated ports.
Bovard said Iran's Foreign Ministry negotiated with China to acquire port facilities and oil terminals, establishing a hub for sanctioned Iranian crude.
Tehran also secured long-term leases on large oil storage facilities in several Chinese locations, allowing it to sell Iranian crude directly in the Chinese market.
Under the arrangement, vessels belonging to Hossein Shamkhani, Ali Shamkhani's son and the owner of a fleet of tankers commonly described as a shadow fleet, transport Iranian oil to docks in China controlled by Tehran. The facilities allow the vessels to continue delivering oil despite US sanctions.
The arrangement is designed to reduce the impact of US sanctions on Hossein Shamkhani's shipping operations. The US Treasury has sanctioned 51 vessels linked to him.
For years, Iran has worked with China to sell oil through trusted intermediaries to small independent Chinese refineries, known as "teapot" refineries. The United States has repeatedly sanctioned companies involved in these transactions, but the use of intermediaries helps shield China's major banks and three largest oil companies from US sanctions.
Iran's oil terminals and storage facilities in China
Two sources in Iran's Oil Ministry told Iran International that Tehran has acquired control of port facilities at three locations in China. One is in the Ningbo-Zhoushan free trade zone, where Iran gained control of a terminal by helping build several smaller transit facilities.
Tehran also secretly acquired stakes in smaller docks at the ports of Qingdao and Pant in China's Shandong province, according to the sources.
The docks are located near pipelines, allowing Iranian crude to reach Chinese refineries quickly without being transferred to other vessels.
Iran has also purchased seven oil storage tanks in China, allowing it to ship crude to the country before securing buyers.
Four large Iranian-owned oil storage tanks are located at the ports of Dalian and Huizhou and in the coastal cities of Dongying and Weifang.
The Oil Ministry controls three other large storage tanks in the Zhoushan area of the Ningbo-Zhoushan archipelago, according to Iran International's sources. They are the Kamergi tank on Aoshan Island, a tank at the Shulanghu Island terminals and another in the Zengyamuo oil zone.
Two months ago, Iran International published a document showing that Mohammad Javad Bavand, a special assistant to the oil minister, instructed oil intermediary Mohammad Hadi Momenin, who owed $2 billion, to use a vessel belonging to Hossein Shamkhani to deliver oil for storage at one of the Chinese ports.
China also earns revenue from storing Iranian oil. Nearly two years ago, Reuters reported that 25 million barrels of Iranian crude were stranded in storage facilities in China and that Tehran had paid $450 million in storage fees.
China distances itself from Iranian oil
Despite these arrangements, the confidential correspondence suggests that Tehran was facing growing pressure from its main oil buyer.
Bovard's confidential letter to Khamenei's office indicates that China had begun distancing itself from Iranian oil even before the 40-day war. According to the letter, Beijing rejected Tehran's request to increase crude oil import quotas for Chinese refineries, increased imports from Venezuela and demanded deeper discounts on Iranian oil.
Two months ago, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the launch of an initiative to economically isolate Iran that China and the United States had more in common than differences. He said China obtained 50 percent of its energy needs from the Persian Gulf and supported the free flow of maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Hossein Shamkhani's grip on Iranian oil trading in Dubai
Throughout the confidential letter, Bovard criticizes Ali Shamkhani, suggesting that his primary concern was protecting his son's interests in the oil trade rather than Iran's oil sales.
Bovard alleged that Hossein Shamkhani used Iranian government loans to purchase vessels but deployed them to transport Russian oil rather than Iranian crude.
According to Bovard, Hossein Shamkhani received Iranian oil on consignment without providing collateral and sold it on the market. Bovard portrayed the United Arab Emirates as Shamkhani's exclusive trading domain, saying the Oil Ministry had effectively become his agent rather than the other way around.
Former lawmaker Ahmad Amirabadi Farahani recently said the then-head of NICO, the National Iranian Oil Company's international trading arm, had barred Hossein Shamkhani and three other oil intermediaries from selling Iranian crude because they owed several billion dollars.
According to Bovard's confidential letter, Ali Shamkhani told Khamenei that Iranian oil had been sold at a discount of 50 cents per barrel under former President Ebrahim Raisi, compared with $9 per barrel under Pezeshkian. The Oil Ministry disputed Shamkhani's figures.
In September, Iran International reported that Mohammad Javad Bavand, a special assistant to the oil minister, had assigned four oil intermediaries, including Hossein Shamkhani, to sell 86 million barrels of Iranian crude at an 8.5 percent discount. The arrangement followed the transfer of oil sales from a network linked to the Intelligence Ministry to one linked to the intelligence arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Oil intermediaries discussed possible collapse of Islamic Republic
Former lawmaker Ahmad Amirabadi Farahani said during a debate that four oil intermediaries met at Charlie restaurant in Dubai hours after Ali Khamenei was killed in US-Israeli strikes. He said they declared that the Islamic Republic was collapsing and that they no longer needed to return proceeds from Iranian oil sales.
The Islamic Republic remained in power, but Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad was later dismissed following Shamkhani's letter to Khamenei.
Two weeks ago, Hossein Ghorbanzadeh, a board member of Persian Gulf Petrochemical Company and an associate of parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, told the Fars news agency that Paknejad's dismissal, carried out three weeks earlier, had originally been planned for Esfand, the Iranian calendar month spanning February and March.
Ghorbanzadeh said President Masoud Pezeshkian had told a cabinet meeting that Khamenei asked him to dismiss Paknejad over his handling of the crisis involving oil intermediaries. Khamenei's death and the outbreak of the 40-day war delayed the dismissal, he said.
